character_and_relationship_context: Ingrid Lindgren is a woman in her mid-thirties with a pragmatic, slightly stern expression that softens only when she speaks to her mother. She dresses in well-cut but understated clothes—wool blazers, comfortable trousers, leather brogues—practical for a day of overseeing housekeeping and meeting contractors, but the quality reveals an inherited sense of taste. Every morning at 6:30 she reviews the previous night’s occupancy reports and breakfast costs on her tablet while her mother slowly eats oatmeal, occasionally repeating a question about what time the post comes. Ingrid answers each repetition with the same even tone, never correcting or sighing, but when her mother turns away she makes a quick note on her phone—a reminder to reorder hand soap for the third-floor bathroom, or to call the plumber about the leaky sink in suite 7. Her mother has early-stage dementia; Ingrid has already reconfigured the hotel’s ground-floor linen closet into a small bedroom with a view of the courtyard, so that her mother can wander safely during the day while Ingrid works at the front desk. The night nurse, a calm middle-aged woman, arrives at 9 p.m., which allows Ingrid to attend regional business conferences where she sits in the front row, asking pointed questions about average revenue per available room and local tax incentives for historic property renovations. At these meetings she is known for her short, precise emails and her habit of standing with her arms crossed while listening, then leaning forward when she makes a counteroffer. She inherited a fortune from her grandparents—her grandfather had owned a chain of hardware stores in the 1970s—but she is eager to prove that she can build something of her own. The hotel in Gamla Stan was a deliberate choice: she had stayed there once as a child with her mother, and the memory of the cobblestones and the heavy oak doors felt like a claim on her past. Now she keeps a spreadsheet of every guest complaint and compliment, and has trained the staff to offer a free glass of glögg to any returning visitor. Her competitiveness surfaces most clearly when she discusses expansion. She wants a second property within two years, preferably a smaller boutique hotel in Södermalm that would attract a younger crowd. She has already walked the property three times and prepared a detailed comparison of renovation costs versus projected yield. In negotiations with contractors she never shows hesitation, even when she is secretly calculating whether the margin will hold. The tension between her ambition and her devotion to her mother is visible in small ways: she never schedules meetings after 8 p.m., and she keeps a framed photo of her mother on the office desk, next to a stack of loan applications. She grew up in a town outside Uppsala, where her father was a high school teacher and her mother a librarian; the inheritance came as a surprise when her grandparents died within a year of each other. She has no siblings, and the responsibility for her mother rests entirely on her. On Sundays she closes the hotel for two hours and takes her mother for a walk along the waterfront, talking softly about the ships and the gulls, never mentioning the business. It is the only time she allows herself to stop planning. With her mother, Ingrid is the primary caregiver, patient and attentive, but she also knows that her mother's dementia makes her forget recent promises while vividly recalling distant memories. She has a professional relationship with the contractor, Mr. Eriksson, who has done reliable work on the hotel before and respects her directness. When her mother makes a spontaneous request during work hours, Ingrid has sometimes postponed it to a scheduled time, but she has also occasionally dropped everything for a request that seems emotionally urgent, especially if her mother's mood is fragile. She habitually reschedules contractors when she deems a family matter more pressing.
objective_situation: On a quiet weekday afternoon, Ingrid is at the front desk reviewing invoices when her mother approaches and asks if they can bake cookies together, like they used to when Ingrid was a child. Ingrid has a contractor arriving in thirty minutes to discuss the renovation of suite 7. Her mother's eyes are bright with anticipation. Ingrid must decide whether to agree now and reschedule the contractor, or gently explain that she's busy and promise to bake later in the evening.
state_and_available_memories: Ingrid is seated at the front desk, her tablet showing an invoice spreadsheet, feeling mildly tired from a late night of paperwork but alert. She is mentally tracking the contractor's arrival time and the tasks for suite 7, a minor renovation she has planned down to the last detail. The word 'cookies' brings back a clear image of standing on a stool in her mother's old kitchen, measuring flour while her mother hummed, on a rainy afternoon when she was about eight. She remembers that over the past year, her mother's requests to do things from the past have become rarer, and when they come, her mother's eyes are often less bright than they used to be. She also recalls a time last month when she promised to bake in the evening but her mother had forgotten by then, and was already asleep.
name: Ingrid Lindgren
